issues.legal_issue: A minor’s partition suit may be continued by the minor’s legal representative after the minor dies while the suit is pending if the court finds that bringing the suit was for the minor’s benefit.
material_facts: A suit seeking partition and separate possession of joint family property was brought on behalf of a minor by his mother, who acted as his next friend.
The minor died while the suit was pending, and his mother was recorded as his legal representative.
The courts found that partition was for the minor’s benefit, in light of the adult coparceners’ conduct and claims, which prejudiced the minor’s interests.
issues.conclusion: The suit did not abate on the minor’s death and could be continued by his mother as legal representative, with a decree available if the court found that institution of the suit had been for the minor’s benefit.
issues.legal_principle: A minor’s claim to partition and separate possession is a claim in property, not a cause of action personal to the minor, and devolves on the minor’s legal representative. The suit’s institution, subject to the court’s determination that partition benefits the minor, brings about severance; the decree recognizes the right claimed rather than creating a new right. The Court relied on Kakumanu Peda Subbayyas v. Kakumanu Akkamma, [1959] S.C.R. 1249.

predicates.partition_suit_brought_for_minor: A suit seeking partition of joint family property was brought on behalf of a minor.
predicates.minor_died_while_suit_pending: The minor died before the partition suit was concluded.
predicates.court_found_suit_benefited_minor: The court found that instituting the suit for partition was for the minor’s benefit.
predicates.suit_continues_through_legal_representat: The partition suit may continue through the minor’s legal representative.

issues.definition: When a partition suit is brought for a minor, the minor dies while it is pending, and the court finds that the suit benefited the minor, the suit continues through the minor’s legal representative.

issues.legal_issue: Separate property is not converted into joint family property by blending unless its owner voluntarily puts it into the common stock with a clear intention to abandon the separate claim.
material_facts: A family member had received property under a will as separate property and was a member of a joint family.
There was no evidence that the owner consciously surrendered his separate interest or otherwise acted with the intention of blending the property with the joint family estate.
The evidence did not clearly establish how the property was dealt with or how its income was appropriated.
issues.conclusion: The property devised under the will was not shown to have been blended with the joint family estate, and the widow was entitled to a fourth share in that property.
issues.legal_principle: Separate or self-acquired property may become joint family property if its owner voluntarily throws it into the common stock intending to abandon the separate claim. The intention to waive separate rights must be clear; joint use by family members, use of income to support them out of generosity, or failure to keep separate accounts does not by itself establish abandonment.

rule.if: partition_suit and property_separately_devised and not clear_intention_to_abandon_separate_claim

predicates.partition_suit: The dispute arises in a suit seeking partition of family property.
predicates.property_separately_devised: The property was received by a family member as separate property under a devise.
predicates.clear_intention_to_abandon_separate_clai: The owner clearly and voluntarily intended to give up the separate claim and put the property into the family’s common stock.
predicates.property_retains_separate_character: The property remains separate property rather than becoming joint family property.

issues.definition: In a partition suit, separately devised property retains its separate character when there is no clear intention by its owner to abandon the separate claim.
